Header:
Date/Time: 2026-04-26 16:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes

Summary:
Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on developer handoff flow from sandbox to pilot. Covered streaming vs sync modes, important generation params for latency/cost tradeoffs, automatic retry/backoff patterns, console shortcuts (Optimize suggestions + per-route histograms), and a short live demo of a graceful failure (model fallback to smaller quantized variant). Gravitas Health cares about data residency, SOC2, and a predictable cost profile. Agreed to run a short 2-week pilot.

Topics:
- onboarding flow: sandbox -> test->pilot
- streaming behavior and client retry patterns
- generation params (temperature, max_tokens, top_p) impact on cost
- batching, prefix/KV cache and when to enable
- model fallback and canary rollouts
- compliance: SOC2 + KMS + data retention options

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Maya (AE): okay woo hello everyone, thanks for taking the time. i'm Maya from Redwood Inference, i'll kick this off and Ethan will run the dev demo.
[00:08] Jordan (Gravitas): hey thanks, we have Priya and Marcus on for infra questions, also Ava for product context.
[00:14] Maya: awesome, quick agenda - 20 min demo of the hosted chat flow and console, then 15-ish on failure modes and ops, and wrap with next steps. sound good?
[00:24] Priya: yep that's good.
[00:26] Ethan (SE): all right i'll share my screen, let me know if the resolution looks off. uh, bear with me while i pull up the sandbox.
[00:34] Ethan: so this is the developer sandbox; we usually tell teams to start here to test prompts and streaming. you'll see the trace pane, token costs per call and an example of prefix caching turned on.
[00:45] Ava: prefix cache? can you explain quickly?
[00:48] Ethan: sure, prefix caching (we sometimes call it KV cache in docs) stores repeated conversation history on the server side so repeated prefixes don't re-run the whole transformer; reduces tokens and latency for multi-turn. note: sometimes the auto transcript writes KV as 'KV cash' in older exports, but it's the cache.
[01:10] Jordan: how does that interact with client-side caching? we have a CDN in front of some endpoints.
[01:15] Ethan: good Q. client-side caching helps for identical requests; Redwood's prefix/KV cache is model-aware and reduces compute, not CDN hits. if you have a CDN, do both but invalidate carefully when prompts change.
[01:30] Marcus: our primary concern is latency at peak; we run sub-200ms SLO for a few flows. can hosted meet that?
[01:38] Maya: short answer: often yes for short responses on our smallest models, but long sequences or larger models can hit 200-500ms. we discuss latency tiers in the console and Optimize will suggest quantized variants and batching thresholds to hit your SLO.
[01:50] Priya: what's the tradeoff vs cost if we pick low-latency?
[01:53] Ethan: lower latency usually means smaller batch sizes, more headroom (reserved or dedicated), and sometimes running a lower-precision quantized model which can slightly impact quality. costs step up because you use more GPU time per qps. we ran a recent benchmark where switching from batch-optimized to low-latency reduced avg latency by ~30% but increased per-token cost by ~22%.
[02:12] Jordan: can you show model fallback? that's a key reliability thing for us.
[02:16] Ethan: yes, i'll show a canary policy. in the console you can define a route with primary model A and fallback model B; if A errors or latency crosses a threshold, traffic automatically spills to B. watch the small test i trigger now.
[02:30] [Ethan triggers a call]
[02:32] Ethan: okay i'm simulating a transient error on the primary model, you'll see the trace switch to the compatible quantized variant and the chat still returns.
[02:40] Ava: nice, can we set percentage rollout?
[02:42] Ethan: yep, canary % and ramp schedule. you can also configure automatic rollback.
[02:48] Jordan: about retries — what does Redwood recommend client-side? simple exponential backoff?
[02:52] Maya: recommended pattern: idempotent retry tokens and exponential backoff with jitter; avoid re-sending non-idempotent requests (like invoice generation) without a unique idempotency key. for streaming, keep the websocket open and implement a resume token if you want to continue from last token.
[03:10] Marcus: are streaming sessions stateful? how do you resume if a socket drops?
[03:15] Ethan: the runtime keeps per-session KV state for a short eviction window; recommended approach is to persist the last good checkpoint (a small KV token or last prompt id) and call the resume endpoint or re-hydrate on reconnect. full long-term state should live in your app DB.
[03:34] Priya: security — do you support customer-managed KMS or HSM?
[03:38] Maya: yes, for Private and Dedicated we can integrate with your KMS/HSM; for Hosted we offer bring-your-key with envelope encryption in some regions — if compliance needs full KMS control we normally recommend Redwood Private.
[03:51] Priya: SOC2?
[03:53] Maya: we are SOC2 Type II and can provide the attestation; we'll share the security pack. also SSO via SAML/OKTA and RBAC for multi-team access.
[04:00] Jordan: good. can we do an initial pilot on hosted but with strict retention?
[04:04] Ethan: yes; hosted can be configured with reduced retention windows and stricter logging controls by route. we'll include that in the pilot template.
[04:14] Ethan: now i'll switch to a quick code sample — this is the simple streaming websocket flow. notice we set stream=true and include an idempotency key. the client receives incremental tokens.
[04:30] [screen shows code snippet]
[04:32] Ava: any gotchas with common JS clients?
[04:35] Ethan: older libs sometimes treat backpressure poorly — important to use a stream consumer with a small buffer and to respect 'isFinal' flags to avoid double-processing fragments.
[04:46] Jordan: show us how Optimize surfaces batching suggestions.
[04:49] Ethan: sure, in the console Optimize tab we ingest traces and recommend batching size, cache thresholds, and quantization level for each route. for example, it suggests enabling prefix cache for routes with >3 turns average and reducing temperature for release-note style generation to reduce token churn.
[05:12] Priya: you mentioned quantization — do you do 4-bit/out-of-the-box?
[05:16] Ethan: we support multiple quantization profiles. 4-bit (QLoRA/LLM-int8-like) is available for many open models; Optimize will recommend which profile based on your eval set. there can be a tiny delta in quality.
[05:29] Marcus: what's the policy for model updates — if you push a new model patch will it break things?
[05:33] Maya: we separate model versions and deployments. you pin a model hash on a route; by default we don't auto-upgrade. updates are rolled out via canaries and optional automatic rollback on quality regressions if you wire up eval checks.
[05:47] Priya: eval checks, like how?
[05:49] Ethan: you attach a prompt set (we call it an eval suite) and Redwood runs periodic checks comparing metrics (BLEU-ish and custom QA pass rates) on candidate deploys. if a candidate falls below a threshold we won't promote it.
[06:03] Jordan: OK can we talk about cost estimation: how do we get from token counts to expected bill?
[06:07] Maya: console shows per-route historical per-token cost and expected spend based on qps and sequence length. Optimize will also output estimated cost delta for each suggestion. we'll send a sample cost model spreadsheet.
[06:22] Ava: for pilot sizing what do you recommend?
[06:24] Ethan: start with a small set of routes (2-3) that represent the extremes (one low-latency short response, one high-context long response). run them against real prompt sets for 3-7 days to get realistic token distributions.
[06:38] Jordan: we have PHI concerns — can we do hosted with data masking?
[06:43] Maya: yes, you can layer data masking and redaction before sending to our API; for PHI we usually recommend private deployment but for experiments we can enable strict retention and show you the flow.
[06:55] Priya: show me a failure mode again — maybe a rate spike.
[06:58] Ethan: right now i'll simulate a sudden qps spike; primary model will hit rate limit and you'll see automatic fallback to the reserve pool.
[07:08] [simulation plays]
[07:12] Ethan: ok, the route went to fallback; the client observed a slightly higher latency but the session completed. trace shows automatic rate-limit-based routing.
[07:20] Marcus: did you lose tokens in that switch?
[07:23] Ethan: not if you use resume tokens; if not, there can be a re-emit of last fragment so we recommend idempotency keys and resume support.
[07:33] Jordan: can we pre-warm models for certain times of day?
[07:36] Maya: yes, pre-warming and reserved capacity are supported — Redwood Dedicated is the option for large predictable peaks, but hosted offers scheduled warm-up hints and auto-bursting to cover short spikes.
[07:49] Priya: we have regulatory requirement that certain geographic data never leaves EU. can we restrict region?
[07:55] Maya: yes — for hosted we have region-restricted endpoints in EU regions; for strict data residency we normally advise Private deployments in your VPC.
[08:06] Ava: small question — how do we instrument for alerting?
[08:09] Ethan: console can push metrics to Datadog/Prometheus; we emit per-route latency, error-rate, and per-token cost. you can wire alerts on top of those.
[08:20] Jordan: competitor question — how do you compare to Anthropic on cost/latency? not naming specifics but want the practical difference.
[08:26] Maya: high level: Anthropic often focuses on model safety/guardrails, we focus on operational predictability and multi-deployment flexibility. you can often get lower unit cost on Redwood for open models with quantization and Optimize tuning.
[08:38] Priya: ok thanks.
[08:40] Ethan: switching back to demo, i'll show a sample failure-rescue script we recommend integrating in the client: short-circuit to a cached reply (for well-known prompts), otherwise attempt two retries with exponential backoff, then call a fallback route.
[08:57] [screen shows sample retry pseudocode]
[09:00] Jordan: any known gotchas when using websockets through enterprise proxies?
[09:04] Marcus: yes our proxies often cut websockets at 60s, that's a problem.
[09:07] Ethan: right, in that case we recommend chunked HTTP streaming or short-lived session tokens and a resume protocol to re-establish with the next chunk.
[09:20] Priya: how will Redwood support our engineers during pilot?
[09:23] Maya: we'll assign an SE for hands-on support (Ethan for the pilot), 2 office hours/week for the first 2 weeks and Slack channel for quick triage.
[09:33] Ava: can Optimize's suggestions be exported? we want to feed them into our infra backlog.
[09:37] Ethan: yes, exportable CSVs and direct links to console recommendations.
[09:42] Jordan: let's do a quick walkthrough of a real prompt from our app — Jordan reads a user prompt about a discharge summary generation.
[09:52] [Jordan shares prompt]
[09:55] Ethan: running live in sandbox — note i set temperature=0.2, max_tokens=160, stream=true. you can see result streaming.
[10:10] [result streams slowly]
[10:15] Ava: that looks pretty good. how sensitive is that to temperature?
[10:18] Ethan: small changes in temperature reduce hallucinations but also lower creativity. for medical notes we recommend 0-0.3 range.
[10:27] Priya: can we set hard length limits to prevent runaway tokens?
[10:30] Ethan: yes, max_tokens caps length and we also support stop sequences and token quotas per route.
[10:37] Jordan: ok can you show how rollback looks if a new model reduces quality?
[10:41] Ethan: sure — here's a canary deploy that runs 10% of traffic through the new model plus the eval suite. if the eval fails we auto-roll back.
[10:53] Maya: quick pause — any other major blockers we haven't covered?
[10:56] Priya: I want to see the security pack and KMS integration details.
[10:59] Maya: noted, we'll attach that.
[11:02] Marcus: confirm pilot scope: we want 3 routes, one low-latency, one long-context, one multi-turn sensitive. can you support that?
[11:08] Ethan: yep that's perfect and will give Optimize enough variety.
[11:12] Jordan: how do we measure quality regressions for subjective metrics?
[11:15] Ethan: attach human eval labels and custom pass/fail rules in the eval suite; Redwood will track regression alerts and tie to rollout rules.
[11:25] Ava: any billing quirks for streaming vs non-streaming?
[11:28] Maya: billing is per-output token for hosted; streaming doesn't add extra token units but longer-lived sessions with keep-alives can cause slight billing interactions if you send heartbeats as real tokens. we recommend separate health pings.
[11:42] Priya: OK last thing — procurement lead time?
[11:45] Maya: hosted pilot can start on a PO or with a pilot agreement; enterprise contracts take longer but pilots are quick — we typically start within 5-10 business days once paperwork and security checks are OK.
[11:58] Jordan: great.
[12:00] Maya: recap — we'll send pricing and pilot template, SE will send benchmark checklist, customer sends prompt set, security pack to be shared. schedule kickoff week of May 10.
[12:12] Priya: sounds good.
[12:14] Maya: any final questions?
[12:16] Ava: none from me.
[12:17] Jordan: that's it, thanks everyone.
[12:20] Maya: thanks all.
